# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Hypothesis: In cytarabine-residual AML that retains oxidative metabolism, an intact differentiation block, and salvage capacity insufficient to compensate blockade of de novo pyrimidine synthesis, atovaquone at verified achievable unbound exposure will inhibit respiratory complex III, shrink the oxidized ubiquinone pool, and restrict DHODH flux, thereby inducing genotype-confirmed myeloid maturation and reducing leukemia-propagating capacity. The mediator is pyrimidine depletion, not generalized ATP collapse. Original indication: treatment and prophylaxis of Pneumocystis pneumonia, and atovaquone–proguanil for malaria; these label facts, reported very high plasma protein binding, and any mammalian complex III potency are unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation before any exposure claim.

Supported premises: Cyatarabine-resistant cells in studied models were not consistently enriched for quiescent leukemia stem cells but showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked oxidative metabolism, with response altered by changing that state [S2]. Separately, DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in experimental AML [S4]. Neither study shows that oxidative residual cells are DHODH-dependent or salvage-limited; that gap becomes a go/no-go gate. ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia stem cells are a distinct selectivity benchmark tested as a separate arm, not a synonym for residual disease [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is only the established metabolic comparator [S3] and is not the proposed finding.

Speculative bridges, explicitly uncertain: (1) partial complex III inhibition will restrict DHODH before meaningful energetic failure, contingent on demonstrated separation of pyrimidine and ATP dose–response curves; (2) salvage-limited residual cells will mature under this restriction while normal progenitors keep function; (3) biochemical premises — human DHODH uses oxidized ubiquinone, uridine salvage can bypass de novo synthesis, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae URA1 is a cytosolic, fumarate-linked, respiratory-chain-independent DHODH — are unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide (active metabolite of leflunomide, rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; unverified) serves as the reference DHODH inhibitor, not the repurposing claim.

Preclinical strategy. Stage 0 feasibility, before any specimens: translate verified atovaquone PK (total Cmax, free fraction) into an unbound ceiling, and run an upfront titration in a reference AML line measuring dihydroorotate-to-orotate ratio, ubiquinone redox state, DHODH flux, oxygen consumption, and ATP rate versus free atovaquone. The project stops with exposure-limited failure if the free EC50 for a DHODH-restrictive shift exceeds achievable unbound Cmax, and the pyrimidine-before-ATP framing is abandoned if those curves do not separate. Stage 1 gates on the same primary specimens after cytarabine pulse and washout, with matched pretreatment bulk blasts, the ROS-low stem-cell arm [S1], and normal CD34+ cells in a comparably cycling state. Prespecified eligibility, fixed before response testing: genotype-confirmed blast morphology with CD11b and CD14 each below 20%; elevated respiration validated by isotope-traced fatty-acid oxidation and genetic perturbation, not etomoxir alone; proliferation recorded as a covariate; salvage limitation defined by isotope partitioning of UTP synthesis under physiological uridine plus a functional test that physiologic uridine repletion fails to maintain UTP pools and proliferation during partial de novo blockade — specimens whose salvage fully compensates are excluded. Go/no-go: teriflunomide in protein-containing medium must raise dihydroorotate-to-orotate at least twofold and CD11b by at least 15 percentage points with ATP within 20% of vehicle and uridine reversing both; failure aborts the atovaquone test in that context. Isolated-enzyme assays must show atovaquone inhibits complex III and spares DHODH, teriflunomide the reverse. A time-resolved gate must show ubiquinone reduction and pyrimidine-flux change while ATP loss remains under 20% and before marker shifts; coincident ATP collapse makes the run uninterpretable and stops it. Decisive rescue: inducible URA1, expressed only after the residual state is established, with proof that pyrimidine restoration leaves complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact; uridine and URA1 must each first reverse teriflunomide — if either fails, stop — and both must prevent atovaquone-induced maturation and clonogenic loss without restoring respiration. Selectivity is a measured outcome, not an assumed window: quantify DHODH flux and salvage capacity in matched normal CD34+ cells and report the AML-versus-normal therapeutic index. Only after all gates, cytarabine-primed xenografts test marrow free drug, longitudinal genotype-resolved fate tracking with absolute counts of mature and immature genotype-positive cells to exclude selective survival of pre-existing mature cells, limiting-dilution secondary-transplant initiating frequency with a prespecified at-least-threefold reduction, and normal hematopoietic recovery. A documented search must position this residual-state, salvage-gated, ubiquinone-timed mechanism against any published atovaquone or leflunomide AML work; this packet does not establish novelty.

Alternatives and falsification: apparent maturation could reflect preferential loss of immature cells, delayed cytarabine injury, direct DHODH binding, other atovaquone targets, or ATP-collapse cytotoxicity, addressed by fate tracking, enzyme assays, titration curves, and rescue. The drug–mechanism–context relationship is falsified — even if atovaquone remains cytotoxic — if validated uridine and URA1 rescues restore pyrimidine pools while leaving complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact and reverse teriflunomide, yet differentiation and at least threefold clonogenic loss persist. Differentiation occurring only above achievable unbound exposure rejects translational feasibility; comparable normal-progenitor injury at the same free EC50 rejects predicted selectivity.

Limitations: high protein binding may leave no free-drug window; cycling normal progenitors share complex III and de novo pyrimidine dependence, so any selectivity margin is an empirical result; differentiation need not durably control leukemia; [S2] models may not match clinical marrow; [S4] may not transfer across genotypes; physiologic uridine availability and murine pyrimidine metabolism may diverge from culture and human settings; all label, exposure, and biochemistry claims above require external verification.

Ranked proposal:
Atovaquone restricts ubiquinone-dependent DHODH to induce differentiation in salvage-limited cytarabine-residual AML, gated by a pyrimidine-before-ATP separation
